title: Handling Difficult Students The First Week Of School school/
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin warns against the common practice of proactively researching and preparing for students with reputations for misbehavior before the school year even starts. He argues this creates a self-fulfilling prophecy: students who feel labeled from day one tend to live up to that label. He offers five specific don'ts: don't seat them closest to you, don't spend more time with them, don't speak to them differently, don't bring up the previous year, and don't ignore their less serious misbehavior. Each of these signals, subtly or overtly, that the student is different or incapable of behaving like everyone else. He concludes that treating reputedly difficult students with the same standard as everyone else, from the very first day, is what allows for lasting change.
points: Researching a student's reputation before the school year starts can create a self-fulfilling prophecy of misbehavior.
Seating a reputedly difficult student closest to the teacher signals distrust and reinforces their expectation of being singled out.
Giving extra check-ins or attention, or speaking differently to a labeled student, communicates distrust even unintentionally.
Bringing up a student's previous-year behavior problems puts teacher and student at odds from the outset.
Ignoring minor misbehavior from labeled students, rather than holding them to the same standard, reinforces misbehavior as their identity.
quotes: And when students feel labeled, they’re pulled inexorably in its direction—fulfilling the prophecy it foretells.
When a student with a difficult reputation walks in on the first day and is asked to sit closest to the teacher, she knows the score.
Your extra attention and frequent check-ins communicate loud and clear that you’ve got your eye on them, creating a distrustful relationship right from the get-go.
It’s common for teachers to speak to difficult students differently than others—without even realizing it.
By way of warning, it’s a common tactic to let difficult students know—in no uncertain terms—that you’re aware of their previous behavior problems. But this undermines your ability to build rapport.
Lasting change happens when we show students, when we prove to them, through our actions and our commitment to the same soaring standards as everyone else . . . That we believe in them.
